properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Alex's idea (who:alex), for his work project, relayed by Anthony in the dev_reflow2 hub session on 2026-09-26:

"I am sort of wondering for work though if I could move it to an ec2 instance and expose it and then add it to the mcp list in my project so coworkers don't need to install reflow2."

Anthony's reading: Alex does not much like the local client (option #2, `reflow2-mcp --remote`), so this is his way of making the direct connection (option #1) work for a team — the same shape as flo2's api.flo2.io, but on the company's own machine.

THE IDEA: one reflow2 on an EC2 instance, `reflow2-mcp --http <addr> --http-allow-host <name> --registry-root <dir>` (or the published container), the team's design imported into it once (an import into an empty store keeps the design's identity). The repo's `.mcp.json` (Claude Code) or Grok Build config lists `https://<name>/g/<id>/mcp`; a coworker opens the repo and their agent connects. Nothing to install, one place to upgrade, and everyone always on the same version.

WHAT IS CHEAP ABOUT IT: almost all of it is built. `--http`, `--http-allow-host` (cap:remote-sessions, verified) and the registry root serving `/g/<graph_id>/` are what flo2's droplet runs today. One process with many clients is one writer, so the single-writer store is fine. Sizing from flo2's droplet: 17 MB per process plus ~5 MB per open design, but CONCURRENT AGENT SESSIONS were observed at 0.5–1 GB each — size the instance by how many coworkers work at once. And the design stays on a company-controlled machine, which is a better home for work content than a personal service like flo2.

COUNTER-ARGUMENTS, RECORDED BESIDE IT:

🛑 1. "EXPOSE IT" IS THE PART THAT CANNOT BE DONE AS STATED. reflow2 authenticates nothing: `--http`'s own help says anything that can reach the port can write the design. On a public EC2 address that is the whole internet. Something in front has to decide who may reach it (dec:idea-authentication-is-somebody-elses-layer-and-the-line-is-the-contributor-id), cheapest first:
   · the company network only — a security group that admits the office or VPN range and nothing else. No code, no key; coworkers are on the VPN anyway. Cheapest by far.
   · a reverse proxy (Caddy, nginx, an AWS load balancer) with TLS that checks a shared team key sent as a header — both Claude Code's `.mcp.json` (`"headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer ${TEAM_KEY}"}`) and Grok Build's `--header` can send one from an environment variable. Cheap.
   · the company's single sign-on in front (an OIDC proxy). The largest, and the only one that knows WHO each person is.

2. A SHARED KEY SAYS WHICH TEAM, NEVER WHICH PERSON. With a VPN or one team key, every coworker's write looks the same to reflow2. Credit per person needs each session to say who it writes for (the `writes_for` tool, v0.71.0) — taken on trust, fine among coworkers — or the SSO option passing identity through, which is what flo2 does. Settling intent (approving) stays the owner's word either way.

3. THE FILES — AND THIS IS THE REASON OPTION #2 EXISTS, so it is worth being plain about. Connected directly, the tools that touch files act on the EC2 instance's disk, not the coworker's: the design export lands on the server, not in the repo; registering and measuring a code file looks for it on the server. If the work repo commits `docs/design/*.json` and runs reflow2's design check in CI, that stops working, or someone has to bring the export back into the repo by hand. If the team keeps the design ONLY on the server and runs no design check in CI, none of this matters. The local client is not "running reflow2 locally": it is a small pass-through that makes the files land on the coworker's machine — but it IS an install, which is exactly what Alex wants to avoid. Zero install gives up the files; a small install keeps them.

4. IT RE-OPENS WHAT dec:central-host SETTLED. That decision (2026-08-26) chose option (c) — a hosted read/publish surface with WRITES KEPT LOCAL — over option (b), a hosted server that holds the writes. This idea is option (b) for a team. flo2 has since shown that hosted writes work in practice (api.flo2.io, with an authenticating gateway in front), so (b) deserves re-weighing — but it is a re-weighing, and should be taken as one.

5. ONE MACHINE, ONE PLACE TO LOSE IT: backups of the store become the team's job (flo2's nightly tarball is the pattern), and an instance that is down is a design nobody can reach — where today each clone carries the design with it.

2026-09-28, A FURTHER SIGHTING: IT WAS DONE, AND THE NEXT QUESTION IS WHETHER REFLOW2 SHIPS THE RECIPE. RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Alex's GitHub issue #616 (art:github-issue-616-oauth-resource-server) reports his team of about 8 running this idea for real: reflow2 0.70.0 in a container on a managed Kubernetes cluster, behind a reverse proxy and an OIDC identity provider, sharing one 1,173-node design. The authentication half of that issue is handled separately. His "hosting notes, offered as a drive-by", in his words: "Things we hit that might be worth a line in the docs, since anyone containerizing this will hit them too":
· "Mount the parent of the store, not the store."
· "A StatefulSet, not a Deployment: a rolling update briefly runs two pods and the second can't take the lock."
· "--http-allow-host is mandatory behind any proxy, and its absence presents as a broken ingress rather than as a rejected Host header."

WHAT ACCEPTED INTENT ALREADY SAYS, searched before framing anything as open:
· dec:backup-belongs-to-the-consumer (accepted): what reflow2 owes a hosting consumer is "a documented update path and honest primitives". A hosting page is in that spirit.
· req:reflow2-consumable-as-an-image (accepted): "reflow2 needs no knowledge of their deploy". Any recipe states RULES an orchestrator must honour, not one platform's deploy.
· dec:the-registry-root-is-the-tenant-boundary (accepted) and the image's label: no authentication, "deploy on a private network, behind a gateway that does authenticate". So any recipe assumes a gateway in front, and which gateway is not answered here.
The Dockerfile's comments already carry most of these rules, and Alex read them ("Your Dockerfile notes do warn about this") and still hit them.

WHAT MEASURING HIS NOTES FOUND, the same day: two of the three are DEFECTS, not missing documentation.
· A --registry-root server drops a store that lost its identity file and says "no designs": fact:root-cause-the-registry-drops-a-store-without-identity-and-says-no-designs-2026-09-28. The single-design path refuses it loudly, and the Dockerfile's warning still describes the pre-guard behaviour.
· A second server on a held store serves the degraded surface, never retries, and passes the image's TCP HEALTHCHECK: fact:root-cause-a-server-degraded-by-a-held-lock-never-retries-and-looks-alive-2026-09-28.
· The Host refusal is the MCP library's opaque 403, and the flag is named only in a startup line: fact:root-cause-the-host-refusal-is-the-librarys-opaque-403-and-the-fix-is-named-only-at-startup-2026-09-28.

OPTIONS FOR THE RECIPE, NONE CHOSEN:
(a) THE RULES AS A PAGE (docs/hosting.md, or the Dockerfile header lifted into docs, linked from the README):
  - mount the parent;
  - exactly one replica and no overlap on update (a StatefulSet, or a Recreate strategy);
  - --http-allow-host names the ingress host;
  - a TCP health probe, not HTTP;
  - an authenticating gateway in front;
  - backups are the consumer's;
  - a real block volume, not NFS.
  Small, and platform-neutral.
(b) A WORKED EXAMPLE FOR ONE ORCHESTRATOR: Kubernetes manifests (StatefulSet, Service, probes), perhaps smoke-tested in CI on a throwaway cluster. Medium to large, and it ties reflow2 to one platform.
(c) FIX THE DEFECTS SO THE RULEBOOK SHRINKS: the registry names an unnamed store; the Host refusal names the flag, and there is a health route the allowlist does not block, or one that tells a degraded server from a served one; a degraded server retries or exits when its cause can clear. Then (a) needs only the rules that are genuinely the operator's. Medium, and it answers the three findings.
(d) NOTHING NEW: the Dockerfile's comments stand as the documentation.

COUNTER-ARGUMENTS, RECORDED BESIDE IT:
· Documenting around a defect makes the page wrong the day the defect is fixed, which is exactly what happened to the Dockerfile's sidecar warning after 2026-08-07. So (c) before or with (a).
· (b) edges against req:reflow2-consumable-as-an-image ("no knowledge of their deploy"), and one orchestrator's manifests read as the supported way when they are only one way.
· Comments in a Dockerfile reach only the person who opens it. Alex did, and the notes still cost his team time. So (d) is measured insufficient for at least one real team.
· Fewer things well (dec:idea-reflow2-does-fewer-things-and-does-them-really-well): a hosting page is small and serves a real consumer. A maintained deployment example is the kind of breadth that question asks about.

═══ 2026-10-01 — @AJS'S WORKPLACE CASE, THE SAME QUESTION (recorded as brainstorming; nothing chosen) ═══
His "project brain" deck lists as open: "Where it would run here — our own machines or hosted; access per repo". The workplace is a national laboratory. Some repos are access-restricted (ansible, ioc_host_vars), and the code and configs describe control-system hosts.

DELIVERY OPTIONS:
(a) LOCAL, PER DEVELOPER, as today: a design per repo, kept with the repo. Nothing to run, but nothing shared live.
(b) ONE SHARED reflow2 INSIDE THE FACILITY: Alex's EC2 shape on a lab machine. It uses the container (req:reflow2-consumable-as-an-image), --http plus the registry root, and the lab's own single sign-on as the OAuth issuer. That is exactly #616's case (an outside team on EKS behind Keycloak), so #616's fixes are this option's path: three merged, #620 in flight.
(c) A SELF-HOSTED flo2 inside the facility, for the account page, sharing, hubs and personas. flo2 assumes one public instance (Clerk, one droplet). Recorded on flo2's side as dec:idea-an-organization-runs-its-own-flo2.
(d) flo2.io, HOSTED: the least to run, and the most likely to be refused by facility data rules.
(e) A HYBRID: each repo's design stays inside the facility, and only a hub that names them is shared.

ACCESS PER REPO is already the model in every option: membership per design (flo2), or a server per design or registry (reflow2). A restricted repo gets its own design with its own members, and a hub never shares its children.

⚠️ THE COUNTER THAT MOVES THE QUESTION: the AGENT is itself an off-site service. Whatever runs the design, the design's text goes to whichever model the developer uses. So "where it runs" is also "which AI the facility permits". reflow2 is model-agnostic (MCP), which keeps an on-premises model possible, but that choice is the facility's, and it decides more than the server does. (@ajs's hxm_program already carries an AI_DISCLOSURE.md.)

SIZES: (a) none. (b) medium, mostly built: it needs #616 finished and an IdP. (e) small on top of (a) or (b). (c) large. (d) small technically, and probably blocked by policy.
properties.name: OPEN — can a team run one reflow2 on its own cloud server (an EC2 instance), list it in the project's MCP config, and have coworkers use it with nothing installed?
